warmup.q: A transactional producer writes 14 ledger entries, then aborts the transaction. A downstream consumer of the ledger topic uses default settings. What does it see?
options: Nothing: aborted records are deleted from the log
Nothing: transactional records only reach the log on commit
warmup.why: Transactional records are written to the log at once, before the decision; an abort only adds a marker. Hiding aborted records is the reader's job, and only a read_committed consumer does it. The default is read_uncommitted, which returns everything. The first and third options are the common belief that an abort removes or never writes the records.

sections.h: A crash between two writes duplicates the output
sections.html:
Most services in a payments platform do the same thing: read a record, work something out, write a record. The ledger service reads payments and writes a debit entry to ledger-entries for each payment. This read-transform-write shape is called consume-transform-produce.

Count the writes per batch. The entries go to ledger-entries. The group's new offset goes to __consumer_offsets, from lesson 6 of this track. Those are separate writes to separate partitions, possibly on separate brokers, and nothing ties them together. If the service dies after writing some entries and before committing the offset, the next instance starts at the old offset and writes those entries again. The Try-it shows it: instance 1 writes four entries and dies, and ledger-entries ends with 10 entries for 6 payments.

The idempotent producer from lesson 5 doesn't prevent this. It drops a retry of the same batch from the same producer session, recognised by producer id and sequence number. Instance 2 is a new producer with a new producer id, and its entries are new records.

Lesson 6 solved this problem at the far end: the ledger checks an idempotency key in the same database transaction as the balance update. That still works, but here it would have to be repeated in every consumer of ledger-entries: the balance service, the statement service, the reconciliation job. Each would need its own dedupe table.

Since both sides are Kafka, there is a better option. If the entries and the offset commit were one write, all of it or none of it, a crash couldn't leave half a batch behind. A Kafka transaction is that one write. It covers records sent to any number of partitions, plus the consumer group's offset commit, and it commits or aborts all of them together.

try.title: Crash a ledger service between its writes
steps: From the labs folder, start the broker: docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait.

Instance 1 * crashes after writing four entries, before it commits; instance 2 takes over from the committed offset. * Argument: "plain" (the default: a normal producer, then commitSync) or "txn" (entries and offsets in one transaction). */ public class LedgerDemo { static final String BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"; static String group; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean txn = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("txn"); long run = System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000; TopicPartition input = new TopicPartition("payments-" + run, 0); TopicPartition output = new TopicPartition("ledger-entries-" + run, 0); try (var admin = Admin.create(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP))) { admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(input.topic(), 1, (short) 1), new NewTopic(output.topic(), 1, (short) 1))).all().get(); } try (var p = producer(null)) { for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) p.send(new ProducerRecord<>(input.topic(), 0, "acct-" + i, "pay-" + i)).get(); } group = "ledger-" + run; String txnId = "ledger-" + run + "-0"; // one transactional.id per input partition this instance owns // instance 1: four entries reach the broker, then the process dies: no commit, no abort, no close var c1 = consumer(input); var p1 = producer(txn ? txnId : null); if (txn) { p1.initTransactions(); p1.beginTransaction(); } for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : pollAll(c1, 6).subList(0, 4)) p1.send(new ProducerRecord<>(output.topic(), 0, r.key(), "entry:" + r.value())).get(); System.out.println("instance 1: wrote entries for pay-0 .. pay-3" + (txn ? " inside a transaction" : "") + ", then crashed before committing"); // instance 2: same group (and, for txn, the same transactional.id), starts from the committed offset try (var c2 = consumer(input); var p2 = producer(txn ? txnId : null)) { if (txn) { p2.initTransactions(); // aborts what instance 1 left open, and fences instance 1 System.out.println("instance 2: initTransactions() aborted instance 1's open transaction"); p2.beginTransaction(); } System.out.println("instance 2: starts at offset " + c2.position(input)); List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> records = pollAll(c2, 6); long last = -1; for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records) { p2.send(new ProducerRecord<>(output.topic(), 0, r.key(), "entry:" + r.value())); last = r.offset(); } Map<TopicPartition, OffsetAndMetadata> next = Map.of(input, new OffsetAndMetadata(last + 1)); if (txn) { p2.sendOffsetsToTransaction(next, c2.groupMetadata()); // the bookmark rides in the transaction p2.commitTransaction(); } else { p2.flush(); c2.commitSync(next); } System.out.println("instance 2: wrote entries for pay-0 .. pay-5, committed offset " + (last + 1)); } for (String isolation : List.of("read_uncommitted", "read_committed")) { List<String> values = readAll(output, isolation); Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>(); for (String v : values) counts.merge(v.replace("entry:", ""), 1, Integer::sum); System.out.printf("%-16s reader sees %2d entries: %s%n", isolation, values.size(), counts); } } /** Polls until n records have arrived: a first poll on a fresh broker can come back empty. */ static List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> pollAll(KafkaConsumer<String, String> c, int n) { List<ConsumerRecord<String, String>> records = new ArrayList<>(); while (records.size() < n) c.poll(Duration.ofSeconds(1)).forEach(records::add); return records; } static KafkaProducer<String, String> producer(String txnId) { Map<String, Object> config = new HashMap<>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "key.serializer", StringSerializer.class, "value.serializer", StringSerializer.class)); if (txnId != null) config.put("transactional.id", txnId); return new KafkaProducer<>(config); } static KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer(TopicPartition input) { var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "group.id", group, "enable.auto.commit", false, "auto.offset.reset", "earliest", "isolation.level", "read_committed", "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class)); c.assign(List.of(input)); return c; } static List<String> readAll(TopicPartition tp, String isolation) { long end; // the log end; a read_committed reader gets there once no transaction is open try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { end = c.endOffsets(List.of(tp)).get(tp); } try (var c = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(Map.of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP, "isolation.level", isolation, "key.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class, "value.deserializer", StringDeserializer.class))) { c.assign(List.of(tp)); c.seekToBeginning(List.of(tp)); List<String> values = new ArrayList<>(); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + 10_000_000_000L; while (c.position(tp) < end && System.nanoTime() < deadline) c.poll(Duration.ofMillis(200)).forEach(r -> values.add(r.value())); return values; } } }

sections.h: A transaction makes the entries and the bookmark one write
sections.html:
A transaction needs a referee: something that remembers which partitions a transaction has touched and whether it committed. That is the transaction coordinator, one of the brokers, which keeps its state in an internal topic, __transaction_state. The producer finds its coordinator through a name you give it, the transactional.id: a stable name for one producer instance, such as ledger-0. It must survive restarts, because that is how the next instance of the same producer is recognised. Setting it turns on idempotence too.

A transaction has five calls:

  1. initTransactions(), once at start-up: register the id with the coordinator, get a producer id and epoch (lesson 5's numbers that let a broker recognise one producer's retries), and finish whatever an older instance with this id left open.
  2. beginTransaction(): from here on, every send belongs to the transaction.
  3. send(...): the records go to their partitions straight away, like any other, marked as part of an open transaction.
  4. sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, consumer.groupMetadata()): the consumer's commit becomes part of the transaction. The consumer must not commit by itself, so set enable.auto.commit=false.
  5. commitTransaction(): the coordinator records the decision in __transaction_state, then writes a COMMIT marker into every partition the transaction touched, including the group's partition of __consumer_offsets. abortTransaction() writes ABORT markers instead.

The important part is step 3. Records are in the log before the decision. An abort doesn't delete anything; it adds a marker that tells readers to skip what came before. Section 3 shows what that means for readers.

Java
producer.beginTransaction();
try {
    for (ConsumerRecord<String, String> r : records)
        producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("ledger-entries", r.key(), "entry:" + r.value()));
    producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(nextOffsets(records), consumer.groupMetadata());
    producer.commitTransaction();                 // entries and bookmark, together
} catch (ProducerFencedException fenced) {
    throw fenced;                                 // section 4: a newer instance owns the id
} catch (KafkaException e) {
    producer.abortTransaction();                  // nothing of this batch becomes visible
    rewind(consumer, records);                    // seek back: the batch must be read again
}
Kotlin
producer.beginTransaction()
try {
    for (r in records)
        producer.send(ProducerRecord("ledger-entries", r.key(), "entry:${r.value()}"))
    producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(nextOffsets(records), consumer.groupMetadata())
    producer.commitTransaction()                  // entries and bookmark, together
} catch (fenced: ProducerFencedException) {
    throw fenced                                  // section 4: a newer instance owns the id
} catch (e: KafkaException) {
    producer.abortTransaction()                   // nothing of this batch becomes visible
    rewind(consumer, records)                     // seek back: the batch must be read again
}

Don't forget the rewind. After an abort, the consumer's position is still past the batch, because poll moved it (lesson 6). Without a seek back to the start of the batch, the next poll returns the following records and the aborted batch is never written. Kafka 4.0 also asks applications to treat a TimeoutException during a transaction as a reason to abort.

Keep transactions short: one poll batch each. A transaction costs a few extra round trips to the coordinator, so one per record would be slow, and a long one holds back readers, as the next section shows.

sections.h: read_committed readers stop at the last stable offset
sections.html:
The TxnDemo Try-it writes to one partition with a transactional producer and a plain one, and prints what two readers see. After a transaction commits a and b, the partition holds a at offset 0, b at 1, and the COMMIT marker at 2. Markers take an offset like records but are never returned by poll, so a reader sees offsets 0, 1 and then a gap. Next a transaction writes c and aborts: the log now holds c at offset 3 and an ABORT marker at 4. Whether a reader gets c depends on one consumer setting.

isolation.level decides. The default, read_uncommitted, returns every record, including those of aborted and still-open transactions. read_committed returns only records of committed transactions, plus all non-transactional records. Every consumer downstream of a transactional producer must set read_committed, or the transaction protects nothing: the default reader saw c.

A read_committed reader has a second rule. It can't read past the last stable offset (LSO): the first offset of the oldest transaction that is still open. Everything below the LSO is decided; at the LSO the broker doesn't know yet. In step 4 of the demo, an open transaction writes e at offset 6, and a plain producer then writes f at offset 7. f is not in any transaction, yet the read_committed reader stops at 6 and doesn't see it. Kafka returns records in offset order, so it can't hand out f while e is undecided. For that reader, endOffsets returns the LSO, and lag is measured to the LSO.

This is the price of transactions. A transaction that stays open holds back every read_committed reader of every partition it has written to, for every record behind it. A producer that crashes mid-transaction holds them until the coordinator aborts it after transaction.timeout.ms (60 seconds by default), or until a new instance with the same id calls initTransactions. Bugs used to leave some transactions hanging for good, with the LSO stuck and compaction blocked; KIP-890, finished in Kafka 4.0, added broker-side checks against that.

The stepper replays the ledger example on both partitions: the crash, the abort, the commit, and the LSO moving through them.

import java.time.Duration; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Writes to a new one-partition topic with a transactional producer and a plain one, and after each step prints the * partition as a read_uncommitted reader and a read_committed reader see it: offsets, values, and where each stops. */ public class TxnDemo { static final String BOOTSTRAP = "localhost:9092"; static TopicPartition tp; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { tp = new TopicPartition("txn-demo-" + System.currentTimeMillis() % 100_000, 0); try (var admin = Admin.create(Map.<String, Object>of("bootstrap.servers", BOOTSTRAP))) { admin.createTopics(List.of(new NewTopic(tp.topic(), 1, (short) 1))).all().get(); sections.h: Zombies are fenced, but exactly-once ends at Kafka's edge
sections.html:
Instance A of the ledger service stops for 40 seconds: a long garbage-collection pause, or a network partition. The group decides A is gone (lesson 7), and instance B starts with the same transactional id. Then A wakes up and carries on where it was, with a transaction full of entries B has already written. A process that has been replaced but doesn't know it yet is called a zombie.

Kafka stops zombies with the epoch from lesson 5. Each initTransactions() bumps the epoch for its transactional id. The coordinator and the partition leaders remember the newest epoch and refuse anything sent with an older one. That is fencing. In the Try-it, A's next send fails with InvalidProducerEpochException, its commit fails the same way, and its abort fails with ProducerFencedException. The only thing left for A is to close. A reader sees A's committed work and B's, and nothing from A after the fence.

There is a second fence on the consumer side. sendOffsetsToTransaction takes consumer.groupMetadata(), which carries the member's generation, a counter the group moves on at every rebalance (lesson 7). If A was thrown out of the group, its generation is old, and the coordinator refuses its offsets even when the transactional ids differ (KIP-447). That is why one producer per instance is enough, instead of one per input partition. Since Kafka 4.0 (KIP-890), the producer also bumps its epoch at the end of every transaction, which closes gaps where a delayed message from an old transaction could land in a new one. That is why the epoch the Try-it prints jumps from 1 to 4 between A's commit and B's.

Now the boundary. A Kafka transaction covers records written to Kafka and offsets committed to Kafka, nothing else. Suppose the ledger service also calls the card issuer to capture a payment, or inserts a row into Oracle, inside the loop. On an abort-and-retry, the Kafka writes disappear from read_committed views, but the capture and the row don't. They run a second time on the retry. Kafka's exactly-once covers Kafka. For a call or a database write inside the loop you still need lesson 6's tools: an idempotency key sent to the card issuer, or checked in the same database transaction as the effect.

Could Kafka take part in the database's transaction instead? KIP-939 proposes exactly that, two-phase commit with an external system, and it is accepted. It hasn't shipped: its client APIs were removed from the 4.1 and 4.2 release branches before release, and Kafka 4.4's KafkaProducer doesn't have them. Design as if it doesn't exist. Lesson 11 of this track shows the transactional outbox, the usual pattern for writing to a database and Kafka together.

refs.title: Commit removing the KIP-939 two-phase-commit APIs from the 4.2 branch

analogy: A transaction is like a bank teller's batch of slips for one customer: a withdrawal from one account, a deposit to another, and a note in the day book saying which request was handled. The teller writes all of them in pencil as she goes, and only at the end stamps the batch "approved" or "void". Auditors who read only stamped slips (read_committed) see the whole batch or nothing; a clerk who reads pencil too (read_uncommitted) sees voided slips. And while a batch is still in pencil, the careful auditors stop reading at its first slip, even past slips that are already in ink, because they read the book strictly in order. The analogy breaks at the bank's other systems: the stamp covers only slips in this book. If the teller also phoned another bank during the batch, voiding the slips doesn't undo the phone call.
world: Kafka transactions fit the Kafka-to-Kafka services in your platform: a fee calculator reading payments and writing fees, an enrichment step, a router that splits payments by currency. In Quarkus, the SmallRye connector does this with a KafkaTransactions emitter: withTransactionAndAck sends the outputs and the incoming message's offsets in one transaction, and the incoming channel needs commit-strategy=ignore so nothing else commits. Downstream channels set isolation.level=read_committed. Kafka Streams with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 uses the same mechanism (lesson 10 of this track). The services that write to Oracle or call the card issuer are different: there the transaction covers only the Kafka side, so the idempotency key in Oracle from lesson 6 stays, and the issuer call must carry an idempotency key the issuer honours. If a Temporal workflow does the side effects, its activity retries need the same keys.
mistake: Turning on transactions in the producer and forgetting the readers. isolation.level defaults to read_uncommitted, so every downstream consumer that wasn't changed still sees aborted entries and the duplicates the transaction was meant to remove. Close behind: catching the failure, calling abortTransaction() and carrying on without rewinding the consumer, which silently skips the aborted batch; and calling a card issuer or writing to a database inside the transaction and assuming the abort undoes it. The fixes: read_committed on every consumer of a transactional topic, seek back to the batch's first offsets after every abort, and idempotency keys for every effect outside Kafka.

Then answer: an open transaction's first record is at offset 120 of a partition whose log end is 180. Where does a read_committed reader stop, and what does endOffsets return for it?

A read_committed reader gets records // up to 119 and stops there, even for non-transactional records written after 120; endOffsets returns 120, // and its lag is measured to 120.

recap: Consume-transform-produce makes separate writes (outputs, then offsets), so a crash between them duplicates output; the idempotent producer can't help across instances.
A transaction (transactional.id, begin, send, sendOffsetsToTransaction, commit) makes the outputs and the offset commit visible together, or not at all.
Records are in the log before the decision; COMMIT and ABORT markers decide, take an offset each, and leave gaps. Nothing is deleted on abort.
Only read_committed readers hide aborted records, and they stop at the last stable offset, the first offset of the oldest open transaction. The default is read_uncommitted.
initTransactions bumps the epoch and fences zombies; after an abort, rewind the consumer to the batch's start.
Exactly-once covers Kafka topics and offsets only. Calls and database writes inside the loop still need idempotency keys; KIP-939 two-phase commit has not shipped.

explain.prompt: Someone proposes turning on Kafka transactions in the ledger service so that "every payment is posted exactly once". The service reads payments, writes ledger-entries, and inserts a row into Oracle for each payment. Explain what transactions would and wouldn't guarantee, and what else is needed.
explain.answer: Transactions would make the Kafka side atomic: the entries written to ledger-entries and the group's offset commit on payments would become visible together or not at all, so a crash in the middle of a batch wouldn't leave duplicate entries for readers that use read_committed. We'd need a stable transactional.id per instance, so a restarted instance fences its predecessor and aborts its open transaction, a rewind after every abort, and read_committed on every consumer of ledger-entries, or they'd still see aborted entries. Transactions wouldn't cover the Oracle insert. If a batch is aborted and retried, the inserts from the first attempt are already committed in Oracle and would run again. So the Oracle side still needs lesson 6's idempotency key, checked by a unique constraint in the same database transaction as the insert. Kafka can't take part in Oracle's transaction: the two-phase commit proposal, KIP-939, hasn't shipped. And open transactions hold back read_committed readers at the last stable offset, so batches must stay short.

deeper.html:
Why the epoch now moves on every commit. Before Kafka 4.0, a transactional producer kept one epoch for its whole life. The EndTxn request that commits or aborts carried no sequence number, so a delayed commit or abort could arrive after the producer had already started its next transaction and be applied to the wrong one. Jepsen's 2024 analysis of Bufstream found this in Kafka's own protocol as aborted reads and lost writes (KAFKA-17754). KIP-890's second phase, finished in 4.0 and gated by the transaction.version feature, bumps the epoch at the end of every transaction and lets the broker add partitions to a transaction by itself, which closes that gap. The 4.0 upgrade notes also ask applications to abort on TimeoutException and TransactionAbortableException.

How readers skip aborted records cheaply. A read_committed fetch response carries a list of aborted transactions for the fetched range: producer id and first offset. The consumer drops records from those producers between that first offset and the matching ABORT marker. Brokers keep an index of aborted transactions next to each segment (the .txnindex file) so they can answer without scanning.

Kafka Streams. With processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2, Kafka Streams runs this lesson's loop for you: one transactional producer per stream thread, offsets and state-store changelog writes in the same transaction. The same edge applies: a Streams application that calls an external API inside a processor gets no exactly-once for that call.
